question: Will the Kennedy Center's main building be open to the general public on October 2, 2026?

calls.reasoning: The Kennedy Center's main building has been closed to the public since Sept 16, 2026, initially framed as a 7-day safety closure (roof terrace canopy issue, partial ceiling collapse from a Sept 4 storm) subject to weekly reevaluation. Base rate: institutional buildings closed for structural safety issues rarely reopen within ~2.5 weeks, especially with no announced repair completion timeline. More importantly, the Trump-aligned board separately voted (Sept 15) for a full indefinite/multi-year ($257M) renovation closure — the 'temporary' safety closure is widely reported (and argued by plaintiff Beatty) as likely pretextual cover for that longer closure, meaning even resolution of the immediate safety issue doesn't imply reopening. Litigation (Beatty v. Kennedy Center, Judge Cooper) has focused on blocking renaming and requiring 30-days' notice before demolition/major changes — Cooper explicitly declined to order the building reopened and denied an emergency hearing on the closure itself. A Sept 23 status-report deadline may produce more clarity but is unlikely to force reopening by Oct 2 given the pace of federal litigation. No direct prediction market exists for physical reopening; the closest Polymarket/Kalshi contracts price demolition announcements (7-32% by various dates) and are near-misses — a non-demolition outcome doesn't imply the building is open, since it could stay shuttered for renovation without formal demolition. As of Sept 22, the Kennedy Center website still lists Millennium Stage events but recent ones (e.g., Sept 25 Dolly Parton event) are explicitly relocated to the REACH (a separate building that remains open), consistent with the main building staying closed. No news found of any planned reopening date.

Countervailing possibility for YES: the emergency safety closure was explicitly framed as ~1 week, and if the structural issue is resolved and litigation pressure (Beatty's suit argues the building should stay open) forces at least partial reopening, the board's 2-year plan could be stalled/reversed, especially since Trump conditioned the actual 'reconstruction' on a D.C. Circuit ruling on his name that may not come by Oct 2 (i.e., renovation work itself may not have started, leaving room for the building to reopen pending litigation). But the board's own resolution already ordered immediate closure regardless of when reconstruction begins, so absent a court order or board reversal, closure should persist past Oct 2.
